Designing an Ad Serving and Auction System (Google Ads / Meta Ads)

Simulate this design Draw it from memory

Difficulty: Advanced Topics: Real-Time Bidding, Ad Ranking, ML Prediction, Budget Pacing, Fraud Detection Asked at: Google, Meta, Amazon, Microsoft, LinkedIn, Flipkart Ads Prerequisites:Caching, Message Queues, and Scalability

1. Understanding the Problem

An ad system selects and serves the most relevant (and profitable) ad to a user in real-time — within 100ms of a page load. It runs an auction among millions of advertisers for every single ad impression, predicts which ads the user is likely to click, charges advertisers fairly, and tracks conversions. The hard parts: running billions of auctions per day at sub-100ms latency, preventing budget overspend in a distributed system, and detecting click fraud that costs advertisers billions.

Real examples: Google Ads, Meta Ads Manager, Amazon Sponsored Products, LinkedIn Campaign Manager.

2. Naive First Cut

Find the highest bidder with remaining budget, show their ad.

Why this breaks:

  • Highest bid is not the best ad — an ad nobody clicks earns nothing (need predicted click-through rate, or CTR)💡 Click-through rate (CTR) = clicks divided by impressions. If an ad is shown 1,000 times and clicked 20 times its CTR is 2%, and since we are paid per click that number decides what an impression is actually worth.
  • Single SQL query per impression at 1M queries per second (QPS) overwhelms any relational DB💡 QPS is just “how many requests arrive each second.” 1M QPS means a million separate database round trips every second, which is far past what one relational database serves.
  • Budget check + decrement is a race condition — 1000 concurrent auctions can overspend💡 A race condition = two requests read the same value at the same time and both act on it. Here a thousand auctions all read “budget left: $10” and all spend it, so the campaign spends $10,000 it did not have.
  • No targeting — everyone sees the same ad regardless of demographics
  • No conversion tracking — advertisers can’t measure return on investment (ROI)
  • Fraud bots clicking ads drain budgets with no real value

The rest of the doc evolves this into a multi-stage ranking pipeline with real-time budget pacing and fraud detection.

3. Prior Art We’re Drawing From

  • Google Second-Price Auction (GSP) - Generalized second-price auction: the winner pays the minimum bid needed to maintain their position (not their actual bid). This incentivizes truthful bidding — advertisers bid their true value without fear of overpaying. (Google Research)
  • Meta Ad Ranking (Total Value) - Ranks ads by bid x predicted_CTR x quality_score (called “total value”). This means a $1 bid with 10% CTR outranks a $5 bid with 1% CTR. Maximizes both revenue and user experience. (Meta Business Help)
  • LinkedIn Ad Budget Pacing - Uses a PID controller to adjust bid multipliers throughout the day so campaigns spend their daily budget evenly (not all in the first hour). The pacer observes actual spend rate vs expected and throttles/accelerates accordingly. (LinkedIn Engineering)💡 A PID controller is the same feedback loop a thermostat uses: measure how far you are from the target, then nudge the control knob up or down. Here the knob is a bid multiplier and the target is “spend the daily budget evenly across the day.”
  • Google Click Fraud Detection - Multi-layered system: real-time filters (impossible click patterns, bot signatures), offline ML models (anomaly detection on click streams), and manual review. Automatically credits advertisers for invalid clicks. (Google Ad Traffic Quality)

4. Functional Requirements

Core (Top 3)

  1. Serve the highest-value ad for a slot - given a user context and ad placement, run an auction and return the winning ad within 100ms
  2. Track impressions and clicks for billing - record every impression and click event accurately; charge advertisers on click (cost per click, CPC) or impression (cost per mille, CPM)💡 CPC means the advertiser pays only when someone clicks; CPM means they pay per thousand impressions (“mille” is Latin for thousand) whether anyone clicks or not. Which one a campaign uses decides what event we have to record durably.
  3. Manage campaign budgets in real-time - enforce daily and total budgets without overspend even under distributed concurrent auctions

Below the Line

  • Ad targeting (demographics, interests, retargeting)
  • A/B testing for ad creatives
  • Conversion tracking (post-click actions)
  • Reporting dashboards for advertisers
  • Ad approval and policy compliance

5. Non-Functional Requirements

Core

  • Latency: Ad selection P99 (the latency 99% of requests beat) < 100ms (ads are on the critical path of page load)💡 P99 is the slow tail, not the average: 99 out of 100 ad requests finish faster than this number. Averages hide the stalls that make a page feel broken, which is why the budget is written against the tail.
  • Throughput: 1M+ ad auctions per second globally
  • Budget accuracy: Overspend tolerance < 1% (beyond that, the platform absorbs the loss)
  • Availability: 99.99% — ad serving down = zero revenue

Below the Line

  • Click data available for reporting within 5 minutes (near-real-time)
  • ML model refresh every few hours (not real-time retraining)
  • Multi-region serving with geo-targeted ads

6. Core Entities

  • Campaign - an advertiser’s ad buy with budget, schedule, targeting, and bid strategy
  • Ad - a creative (image, text, video) with targeting criteria and a landing page
  • Auction - a single ad slot request that runs ranking across eligible ads
  • Impression - a record that an ad was shown to a user
  • Click - a record that a user clicked an ad
  • BudgetLedger - real-time remaining budget per campaign

7. API / System Interface

GET /v1/ads/serve?slot_id=homepage_banner&user_id=u123&context={page,device,geo}
Response:
{
  "ad_id": "ad_456",
  "creative_url": "https://cdn.example.com/ad456.webp",
  "click_url": "https://track.example.com/click?imp=imp_789",
  "impression_id": "imp_789"
}
// Response within 100ms; fires impression pixel automatically

GET /v1/ads/click?imp=imp_789
Response: 302 Redirect to advertiser landing page
// Server records the click event before redirecting

POST /v1/campaigns (advertiser API)
Body: {"name": "Summer Sale", "budget_daily": 5000, "bid_cpc": 2.50, "targeting": {...}, "ads": [...]}
Response: {"campaign_id": "c_123", "status": "pending_review"}

Security notes: impression and click URLs include signed tokens to prevent forgery. Rate-limit click endpoint per user to prevent manual click fraud. Never trust client-reported impressions — server-side pixel tracking is the source of truth.💡 A signed token is a value the server stamps with a secret so it can later tell whether the value came from us. Without it anyone could invent an impression_id and bill a competitor for clicks that never happened.

8. High-Level Design

FR1: Serve the highest-value ad (auction pipeline)

Read the requirement plainly: given an ad slot and a user, return an ad that someone is willing to pay for. That needs a way to find the ads eligible for this user, a rule for choosing between them, and a check that the advertiser still has money.

Build that and nothing else. Three components, and the choosing rule is the obvious one — whoever bids most wins and pays what they bid. Every refinement below answers a non-functional requirement, so each belongs in a deep dive.

New components we need:

  1. Ad Server - Runs the auction. Takes the slot and user context, gets candidates, picks a winner, returns the creative.
  2. Ad Index - Answers “which ads target this user?” Holds active campaigns keyed by targeting attributes so retrieval is a lookup rather than a scan of every campaign.💡 A search index stores the mapping backwards from how you would expect: instead of “campaign → its targeting,” it keeps “targeting attribute → the campaigns that want it,” so one lookup per attribute replaces reading every campaign.
  3. Budget Service (Redis) - One counter per campaign, decremented atomically before an ad is served. Atomic is not an optimization here: thousands of ad servers decrement the same campaign concurrently, and a read-then-write would let them all pass a check that only one of them should.💡 Atomic = the read and the write happen as one indivisible step that no other request can interleave with. That is what makes “subtract $2.50 and tell me what is left” safe when a thousand servers ask at once.

Flow:

  1. User loads a page → the Ad Server receives the slot id and the user context
  2. Candidate retrieval: query the Ad Index for ads whose targeting matches this user. Returns on the order of 1,000 candidates
  3. Eligibility filter: drop anything out of schedule or already frequency-capped for this user💡 A frequency cap is a per-user limit on how many times the same ad may be shown, e.g. three times a day. It exists because the fourth showing annoys the user and almost never gets clicked.
  4. Pick a winner: sort by bid, highest first. The top bidder wins and is charged its bid
  5. Budget check: DECRBY that campaign’s counter. If it goes negative, put the money back and move to the next candidate
  6. Return the creative URL and a signed click URL to the browser

Why is the budget counter in Redis rather than the campaigns table? Because this check sits inside a 100ms P99 on 1M auctions a second, and it is a read-modify-write on a single hot row. A relational row lock at that contention rate serialises the entire auction fleet behind one campaign. An in-memory atomic counter answers in microseconds and is the one piece of shared mutable state the auction genuinely cannot avoid.

What we have deliberately left broken. This serves ads, charges advertisers, and respects budgets. Four things about it are wrong, and every one of them is a non-functional failure rather than a missing feature:

  • Step 4 ranks on bid alone, which is revenue-blind. We get paid per click, so what a candidate is actually worth is bid × the chance anyone clicks it. Ranking on the first factor and ignoring the second reliably picks the wrong ad. That is Deep Dive 1.
  • Step 4 charges the winner its own bid. First-price pricing punishes anyone who bids what an impression is truly worth, so every advertiser is pushed into guessing games instead of telling us their value. That is Deep Dive 4.
  • Step 5 spends budget as fast as traffic arrives. A campaign with a daily budget and a morning traffic spike is exhausted before lunch and invisible for the rest of the day, which is not what the advertiser bought. That is Deep Dive 2.
  • Nothing here asks whether a click was real. That one surfaces in FR2.

FR2: Track impressions and clicks for billing

An ad we served and nobody paid for is revenue we lost, so impressions and clicks have to be recorded durably. This is the billing record, which makes it the one place in the design where losing a write costs real money.💡 Delivery semantics are the guarantee a pipeline gives you - at-most-once can silently drop an event, at-least-once can hand you the same event twice. Billing cannot use at-most-once, because a dropped click is revenue we never invoice. Learn more →

New components we need:

  1. Event Tracker - Receives the impression pixel and the click redirect, and writes the record.💡 An impression pixel is a tiny invisible image the browser must fetch to render the ad. Because the fetch hits our server, it is proof the ad really appeared rather than the page merely claiming it did.
  2. Billing DB (Postgres) - One row per impression and per click, carrying the auction price that was agreed at serve time.

Flow:

  1. The browser loads the impression pixel → the Event Tracker records that this auction actually rendered
  2. It writes an impression row carrying the auction metadata, including the price the winner agreed to
  3. The user clicks → the click goes through the Event Tracker rather than straight to the advertiser
  4. The tracker writes a click row and charges the advertiser the auction price
  5. It then issues the redirect to the advertiser’s landing page

Why route the click through us at all, rather than linking directly? Because a click is the billable event, and the only way to know it happened is to be in the path when it does. The impression and click URLs carry signed tokens for the same reason: an unsigned click URL is an invitation to forge billable events, and the impression_id has to be something the browser cannot invent.

Why never trust a client-reported impression? The pixel firing is server-observed. A client-supplied “I showed your ad” field would let any page claim arbitrary impressions, so the server-side pixel is the source of truth and the client is never asked.

What we have deliberately left broken. Two holes, and they compound:

  • Every click is billed as genuine. Nothing here asks whether a human did it. A competitor with a script, or a bot farm, can drain a campaign’s daily budget in minutes, and we will bill the advertiser for all of it and report it as performance. That is Deep Dive 3.
  • Step 4 charges inline, on the redirect. The user is waiting on a database write before they reach the page they clicked, and at 1M auctions a second the impression write alone is a write rate no single relational database will absorb. Deep Dive 3 is also where this path becomes a durable event stream, which is what both the throughput problem and the fraud analysis need.

FR3: Budget management

An advertiser sets a daily budget and we must not exceed it. The hard part is that thousands of ad servers spend against the same campaign at the same time, so “check the budget, then spend it” is a race unless the check and the spend are one operation.

New components we need: none. FR1 already introduced the Redis counter, because an auction cannot pick a winner without knowing whether that winner can pay. This section is about what the counter guarantees and where it is reconciled.

Flow:

  1. Before serving a won ad, the Ad Server calls DECRBY campaign:{id}:budget <price>
  2. Redis is single-threaded, so the decrement and the resulting value are one indivisible step. Two servers cannot both see “enough left” for the same last dollar
  3. If the returned value is negative the budget is gone: add the amount back, mark the campaign exhausted, and serve the next candidate instead
  4. A daily job reconciles the counter against what the Billing DB actually charged, which is the authority. Fraud credits from Deep Dive 3 land here
  5. At the campaign’s midnight the job resets the counter to the daily budget

Why does overspend tolerance exist at all, if the counter is atomic? Because the decrement happens at serve time and the charge happens at click time, and the two can disagree. An ad served in the last second of the day can be clicked after the reset. The 1% tolerance in the requirements is the budget for that gap, not sloppiness in the counter.

What we have deliberately left broken. The counter prevents overspending and says nothing about when the money goes:

  • Budget is spent as fast as traffic arrives. A campaign whose audience is most active at 9am exhausts its daily budget during the morning spike and is absent for the remaining fifteen hours. The advertiser paid for a day of exposure and got two hours of it, and the counter was working perfectly the whole time.
  • The fastest bidder wins the day, not the best one. Because exhaustion is first-come-first-served, which campaign gets shown is decided largely by traffic timing rather than by value.

Both are Deep Dive 2.

Budget store Campaign budgets Remaining budget per campaign Atomic decrement at high QPS Redis (in-memory atomic ops) DynamoDB

scroll →

💡 Two acronyms in that table: OLTP (online transaction processing) means lots of small reads and writes of individual rows, like recording one charge, while OLAP (online analytical processing) means scanning millions of rows to total them up, which is what an advertiser dashboard does - and why reporting sits in a separate columnar store instead of the billing database.

Why Redis for budget? Budget decrements happen on every auction win — potentially 100K+/sec per campaign during peak. Redis DECRBY is atomic, single-digit microsecond, and handles this without locks. Postgres row-level locking would bottleneck at 1K/sec per row.

10. Data Modeling

Elasticsearch (Ad Index — candidate retrieval):

Index: active_ads
  _id: ad_id
  Fields: campaign_id, advertiser_id, bid_amount, bid_type (CPC/CPM),
          targeting (nested: { age_range, geo, interests[], device_types[] }),
          creative_url, landing_url, status, quality_score
  Mapping: geo_point for location targeting, keyword for interests

Redis (Budget Store — real-time spend tracking):

Key: "budget:daily:{campaignId}:{date}" → Integer (remaining cents)
Key: "budget:total:{campaignId}" → Integer (remaining total budget in cents)
Operations: DECRBY on auction win, checked before bidding
TTL: daily keys expire after 48 hours

Kafka (Event Stream — impressions and clicks for billing):💡 Kafka is a durable append-only log of events. The ad server writes a click onto the log and moves on; billing, fraud detection and the model trainers each read the same log at their own pace, so a slow consumer never slows the auction. Topic: ad-events (partitioned by campaign_id)
  Key: campaign_id
  Value: { event_type (impression/click), ad_id, user_id, timestamp, 
           slot_id, bid_amount, device, geo }

Postgres (Billing DB — advertiser charges):

CREATE TABLE ad_charges (
    charge_id BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
    campaign_id UUID NOT NULL,
    advertiser_id UUID NOT NULL,
    event_type VARCHAR(10) NOT NULL,  -- click, impression
    amount DECIMAL(10,4) NOT NULL,
    ad_id UUID NOT NULL,
    charged_at TIMESTAMP NOT NULL
);
CREATE INDEX idx_charges_campaign ON ad_charges(campaign_id, charged_at DESC);

Access Patterns:

Query Data Source How
Find eligible ads for slot Elasticsearch Bool query: must match geo + device + interests, filter by active status
Check budget before bid Redis GET budget:daily:{campaignId}:{today} — if <= 0, exclude from auction
Decrement budget on win Redis DECRBY budget:daily:{campaignId}:{today} bidAmount — atomic
Record impression/click Kafka Produce to ad-events topic (fire-and-forget from ad serving path)
Billing aggregation Kafka → Postgres Consumer batches events, inserts to ad_charges every 5 seconds
scroll →

How Budget Pacing Prevents Overspend Under Distributed Auctions:

  1. Campaign has $1000 daily budget. At midnight: SET budget:daily:{campaignId}:{date} 100000000 (in hundredths of cents for precision)
  2. Each auction server checks budget BEFORE bidding: GET budget:daily:{campaignId}:{today} — if ≤ 0, ad is excluded from the auction
  3. On auction win: DECRBY budget:daily:{campaignId}:{today} bidAmount — atomic, no locks
  4. Race condition risk: 10 servers simultaneously read budget=500 and each bids 100. All succeed → overspend by 500.
  5. Mitigation: use DECRBY and check the RETURN value. If result < 0, the decrement already happened but we DON’T serve the ad — absorb the overspend (< 1% tolerance)
  6. For tighter control: Redis Lua script does GET + DECRBY atomically — zero overspend but adds ~1ms latency

11. Deep Dives

1) Ranking by bid picks the wrong ad. How do we rank on expected revenue in under 20ms?

Problem: FR1 sorts candidates by bid. But we are paid per click, so an impression is worth bid × the probability of a click — and FR1 optimizes only the first half of that product.

Bad: rank by bid alone, exactly as FR1 does. Work an example, because the gap is larger than it looks. A luxury-car ad bids $5.00 CPC and converts at a 0.1% CTR, so each impression is worth $5.00 × 0.001 = $0.005. A mobile-game ad bids $1.00 CPC at a 2% CTR, worth $1.00 × 0.02 = $0.02. The cheaper ad is worth four times as much per impression, and FR1 shows the expensive one every single time.

This is not a rounding error on the margin. It is the wrong winner on a large fraction of 1M auctions a second, and it is self-reinforcing: the high-bid, low-CTR ad keeps winning slots it monetises badly, so overall yield stays low while advertisers with genuinely engaging creative get squeezed out by bid alone. A marketplace that rewards bid rather than value also teaches advertisers the wrong lesson about what to optimise.

Predict CTR with a real model and rank by . This is the correct objective, and the naive implementation does not fit the latency budget: 1,000 candidates through a 50ms model is , against a 100ms P99 for the whole page. Even a 1ms model is a full second.

Two-stage. A lightweight model (logistic regression) scores all 1,000 in ~5ms, then the top 50 go to a heavier gradient-boosted model for ~15ms of re-ranking. Total ~20ms, which fits. The limit is that the cheap first stage is doing the consequential filtering, so anything it misranks never reaches the accurate model.

User embeddings are computed once per session and cached. Ad embeddings are pre-computed at campaign creation. At serving time, ranking is a dot-product similarity (user_emb · ad_emb) which is sub-millisecond for 1000 candidates via SIMD. Only the top 20 go through the full feature-rich model. This is how Meta serves 10M+ auctions/sec.

2) An advertiser buys a day of exposure and gets two hours. How do we spread the spend?

Problem: FR3’s counter stops overspending and does nothing about timing. Budget drains at whatever rate traffic arrives, and traffic is not uniform.

Bad: the first-come-first-served drain FR3 built. A campaign with a $5,000 daily budget at a $2.50 CPC can afford 2,000 clicks. If its audience is concentrated in the morning commute, those 2,000 clicks are gone by 9am and the campaign is invisible for the remaining fifteen hours of the day — including the evening, which for most consumer categories converts better than the morning did.

The advertiser’s experience is that they paid for a day and received a spike. Worse, the impressions they did get are the cheapest-converting ones, because exhaustion is decided by traffic timing rather than by value, so the budget is systematically spent on whoever showed up first rather than on whoever was worth the most. And nothing in the system reports this as a problem: the budget was respected exactly.

And nothing in the system reports this as a problem: the budget was respected exactly.

Slice the budget by hour using historical traffic distribution, and cap spend per slice. This fixes the gross failure — the campaign now runs all day. What it cannot do is react: the slices are set from last week’s traffic, so an unexpected news event, a competitor pulling out of the auction, or a holiday makes every slice wrong at once, and the campaign either underspends all day or exhausts a slice in ten minutes and goes dark until the next one opens.

(borrowing from LinkedIn). The pacer observes actual vs target spend rate every minute and adjusts a bid multiplier. Underspend → increase multiplier (bid more). Overspend → decrease. The PID gains are tuned to converge smoothly without oscillation. This handles traffic fluctuations, competitive dynamics, and seasonal patterns without manual hourly budgets.

3) A script can drain a competitor’s daily budget in minutes. How do we only bill real clicks?

Problem: FR2 writes a click row and charges for it. It has no notion of whether a human was involved, and the click endpoint is a public URL.

Bad: bill every click, which is what FR2 does. Put the attack on a clock: a campaign with a $5,000 daily budget at $2.50 a click is exhausted after 2,000 clicks. A single script issuing even 20 requests a second reaches that in under two minutes. One competitor, one afternoon, and a rival’s advertising is off the platform for the day — and we invoice them for the privilege.

The second-order damage is worse than the first. Those fraudulent clicks are also reported to the advertiser as performance, so their measured CTR and conversion rate are corrupted. They will optimise their campaigns against poisoned numbers, conclude the channel does not work, and leave. Fraud that we bill and then report as success does not just steal money, it destroys the measurement the whole marketplace runs on.

It also breaks Deep Dive 1. The CTR model trains on observed clicks, so systematic fraud teaches the ranker that the defrauded ad is highly engaging, and it starts winning more auctions it will never monetise.

Inline rule-based filters — reject known bot IPs and datacentre ranges, the same user clicking the same ad ten times a minute, and clicks arriving implausibly soon after the impression, since under about 50ms no human has read the creative. Cheap, and it catches the unsophisticated majority. It cannot catch a distributed botnet with residential IPs and human-plausible timing, and a static rule is a target: anything a rule rejects deterministically is something an attacker can tune around in an afternoon.

Invalid clicks are excluded from billing retroactively. Advertisers see “invalid clicks filtered” in their reports, building trust.

4) Why does charging the winner its own bid make every advertiser lie to us?

Problem: FR1 charges the winner exactly what it bid. That sounds like the fair and obvious rule, and it makes bidding your true value a strictly losing move.

Bad: the first-price auction FR1 built. Follow the incentive. An advertiser values a click at $5.00. If they bid $5.00 and win, they pay $5.00 and their surplus is zero — winning is worth exactly nothing to them. So they bid below their value, and the only question is how far below.

That turns bidding into a guessing game about everyone else. If the next-highest bid is $2.00, bidding $2.01 captures $2.99 of surplus, so the rational move is to probe downward until they start losing auctions, then creep back up. Every advertiser does this simultaneously, so the thing each is trying to estimate is itself moving. The result is bid oscillation with no stable resting point, and prices that reflect how good an advertiser’s bid-optimisation tooling is rather than how much the inventory is worth.

Two concrete harms for us. The bids we receive are no longer information — we are ranking on a number that is deliberately not the advertiser’s value, which also undermines the bid × pCTR objective from Deep Dive 1 because half of that product is now a strategic fiction. And small advertisers without automated bid management systematically overpay relative to large ones running shading algorithms, which pushes exactly the long tail we need off the platform.

the first-price auction FR1 built. Follow the incentive. An advertiser values a click at . If they bid $5.00 and win, they pay $5.00 and their surplus is — winning is worth exactly nothing to them. So they bid below their value, and the only question is how far below.

That turns bidding into a guessing game about everyone else. If the next-highest bid is $2.00, bidding $2.01 captures of surplus, so the rational move is to probe downward until they start losing auctions, then creep back up. Every advertiser does this simultaneously, so the thing each is trying to estimate is itself moving. The result is bid oscillation with no stable resting point, and prices that reflect how good an advertiser’s bid-optimisation tooling is rather than how much the inventory is worth.

Two concrete harms for us. The bids we receive are no longer information — we are ranking on a number that is deliberately not the advertiser’s value, which also undermines the objective from Deep Dive 1 because half of that product is now a strategic fiction. And small advertisers without automated bid management systematically overpay relative to large ones running shading algorithms, which pushes exactly the long tail we need off the platform.

Second-price — the winner pays just above the second-highest bid. Now bidding true value is the strategy: you cannot do better by shading, because what you pay is set by your competitor rather than by your own bid, and shading only risks losing auctions you wanted to win. Bids become honest signals again. Google ran this for years for exactly this reason. The limit is that it reasons about one slot at a time, and real pages have several.

(Vickrey-Clarke-Groves) for multi-slot scenarios. When showing multiple ads (like a search results page with 4 ad slots), VCG charges each winner based on the externality they impose on others. Mathematically guarantees truthful bidding and maximizes social welfare. In practice, Google shifted to first-price for display ads in 2019 because market dynamics favored transparency over theoretical optimality — but second-price remains for search ads.

12. Design Self-Audit

  • Stale reads? Ad Index refreshes every few minutes (new campaigns appear with slight delay). Budget is real-time via Redis.
  • Single points of failure? Redis budget store is the most critical — replicated with automatic failover. If Redis is briefly unavailable, Ad Servers use local cached budget estimates and reconcile after recovery (may overspend by ~0.5%).
  • Dead-letter / reconciliation? Kafka click events that fail billing processing go to a dead-letter queue (DLQ). A reconciliation job retries and alerts on persistent failures.💡 A dead-letter queue is a side holding area for events that kept failing. Without one, a single malformed click event is retried forever and blocks every click behind it in the partition.
  • Cost at scale? ML inference is the biggest compute cost. Batch inference (scoring 200 candidates per request) amortizes model loading overhead. Feature store read cost is high but cacheable.
  • Hot partition? A viral campaign with massive budget could overwhelm a single Redis key. Mitigation: shard budget across multiple keys (campaign_budget_shard_0..N) and sum on read.💡 A hot partition is one shard that receives far more traffic than its peers, so adding machines does not help - every request still lands on the same one. Splitting a single campaign counter into N sub-counters spreads that load across N shards. Learn more →

13. Core Flows

Flow 1: Ad Auction (full pipeline)

Non-obvious failure path: If ML Ranker is slow (> 50ms), Ad Server falls back to a simpler scoring model (bid x historical CTR from cache). Ads still serve — just with slightly less optimal ranking. Never show a blank ad slot.

14. Final Architecture

How it works end-to-end:

  1. User sends ad request — browser hits the Load Balancer with page context
  2. Ad Server queries the Ad Index — retrieves candidate ads matching targeting criteria
  3. ML Ranker scores candidates — pulls user features from the Feature Store and predicts CTR
  4. Budget check via Redis — Ad Server confirms the winning ad’s campaign still has budget (Budget Pacer keeps this fresh)
  5. Ad is served to user — winning creative returned in <100ms
  6. User interacts (impression/click) — Event Tracker fires the event to Kafka
  7. Billing Processor consumes event — deducts spend from the advertiser’s account in the Billing DB
  8. Fraud Detector consumes event — flags suspicious click patterns for retroactive credit
